feedback: Written before this candidate has raced; no outcome is stated for it. Evidence: iteration 1 (best, 114.4) had oval progress 0.47, max_error 0.061 to 0.066 m, rms_error 0.026 to 0.031 m and oval steering oscillation 0.28. The sensor-footprint and count changes in iterations 2 and 3 cut progress to 0.23 and 0.41, so the iteration-1 array stays the reference. Iteration 4 raised drivetrain speed and gave 110.2, close to iteration 1 but with oscillation rising to 0.33. For this candidate the Integrator changed nothing in the controller: the gains are iteration 1 exactly, so the only variable is the sensor lead, moved from 0.03 m to 0.02 m. Integration point: sensors closer to the axle see the line later on bends, so the controller gets less look-ahead and may react later. Change the next design according to the race. If max_error drops to 0.06 m or below and oval progress is at or above 0.47, keep the 0.02 m lead and try mass 0.55 kg to damp the remaining excursions. If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.3 with no gain in max_error, return the lead to 0.03 m, because iteration 4 showed that extra speed without damping raises oscillation. If line_loss_events rise above the iteration-1 value of 0.3, the lead is too short for the tight bends, so keep 0.03 m and move to a wheel_track change.
requested_changes: If max_error is at or below 0.06 m on the oval and s-bend with oval progress at or above 0.47, keep the lead at 0.02 m and set mass to 0.55 kg (from 0.6). Iteration 4 showed that a lighter body raises oscillation (0.33), so use only a small step.

If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.3 while max_error does not improve, return sensor y to 0.03 m and set wheel_track to 0.11 m (from 0.10). Iteration 0 with a 0.12 m track gave lower oval oscillation (0.085), so this trades some turn authority for damping.
If line_loss_events rise above 0.3 on the slalom or s-bend, keep sensor y at 0.03 m. Iterations 1 and 4 showed the lead of 0.03 m held the line on the tightest bends, so do not shorten it further.
